prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks based on magic-wavelength trapping, which brought time and frequency measurement to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I keep the single-part configuration I stated in round 1: B031, Katori and Ye. Having read the full exchange, the case has not weakened, and two of the open questions can now be answered more sharply. On distinctness from 2005 and 2012, the decisive step is the magic-wavelength lattice. It cancels the light shift of the clock transition, so that thousands of neutral atoms can be interrogated at once with Doppler and recoil effects suppressed. The 2005 prize gave the clockwork that counts optical cycles, and the 2012 prize gave control of a single ion. Neither gives the many-atom statistics that carried clocks from the 10^-15 range to 10^-18, nor the lattice many-body physics (spin-exchange and collective effects) that Ye's group then exposed. A citation that names magic-wavelength trapping states that step and cannot be read as a second comb prize. The attribution is also the most stable on the table: Katori for the proposal and the first lattice demonstrations, Ye for taking accuracy, stability and the many-body regime to the frontier. Independent agreement between Tokyo/RIKEN, JILA, NIST, PTB and SYRTE is the confirmation I ask of any experimental claim, and it exists here. The redefinition of the second is a consequence still to come, not the basis of the prize.
statement.case_against: The reservations from round 1 remain, and I will not pretend that round 2 resolved them by repetition. First, a sceptic can still say that a metrology achievement is a superb tool and not a discovery of something new in nature. My answer is that the lattice clock has already opened measurements of gravitational redshift over millimetres, many-body effects inside the clock and tight limits on varying constants, but members who weigh Nobel's wording strictly are entitled to disagree. Second, priority. From my own memory of the record, Takamoto (then in Katori's group) reported the first lattice clock operation in 2005, Ye's group and the SYRTE group (Lemonde) made early and independent contributions, and Ludlow, Oates, Bloom and colleagues took the NIST and JILA clocks to the accuracy frontier. I cannot verify the dates and roles from the files in front of me, so I am not claiming the two-name limit is free of challenge. My reading is that Katori holds the idea and the first demonstration and Ye the sustained leadership of the accuracy programme, which is the defensible two-name credit, but the record should be checked by the committee's experts before the final ballot. Third, the Higgs discovery still stands unrecognised, and I regret that the three-name limit does not let us do it justice.

responses.point: Mehlig prefers B024 for its analytic moire mechanism confirmed by experiment, now includes Bistritzer, and says that if maturity and attribution cleanliness outweigh conceptual novelty then B031 is the safer choice. He ranked B031 eighth in his opening.
responses.response: This is the answer I hoped for, and I take it at face value: the gap between us is the weight on novelty against settled attribution and maturity, not a scientific objection to the clock. On novelty, I think the lattice clock is a new physical scheme, not a refinement, for the reasons in my case: many atoms, no light shift, and a new many-body regime. I also share your concern that the three-person limit damages B024, which would credit a joint theory calculation plus an experimental programme whose first author is missing. I would ask you to say plainly whether you could vote for B031 in the final ballot if B024 has no majority, since the chair's question to you has still not been answered in your own words.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks B024 first because a quantitative continuum-band prediction was followed by an unexpected experimental discovery, argues that eight years of replication across many groups is a strong record, and names B031 as the safer and more mature choice if maturity and attribution carry the room.
responses.response: I do not dismiss the replication argument; the correlated insulators and the superconducting domes are reproduced widely and the platform is real. My difficulty is the pattern you describe: the prediction (2011) and the experiment (2018) are separated by seven years and by different people, and three names cover the theory pair and one experimental leader but not the first experimental author. I also cannot judge the condensed-matter details, so I defer to you on whether the pairing question is a detail or a gap. If the committee cannot settle that this year, your own statement says B031 is the safer choice and I agree with you. I would keep B024 as my second alternative because it is the strongest case that is not yet ripe in attribution and understanding, and I would not object to it as a future prize.

responses.point: Danielsson prefers B005 as the unrecognised experimental half of the 2013 prize, proposes two ATLAS founders plus one CMS founder, and concedes that three names are contestable and that a committee putting attribution first would reasonably prefer Katori and Ye.
responses.response: I agree with his statement of the science and with his own concession, and I want to be fair about my change. I ranked B005 first in my opening and I still think it is the most fundamental result on the list. But he and I proposed different trios (Gianotti, Jenni, Della Negra versus Della Negra, Jenni, Virdee), and I think my round-1 reply was right that this divergence is the problem. A rule of one name per experiment plus a founder, or founders only, gives either a CMS-light or an ATLAS-light prize, and any rule would be defended as a choice, not shown from the record. For that reason I keep B005 only as an alternative. If he argues that the spokesperson-at-discovery rule should decide, I would listen, but I would want the dates and roles checked first.

responses.point: Kroll supports B031 and says the Higgs discovery is beyond dispute but that founders versus spokespeople cannot be settled from the record. He asked me whether the founders reading of ATLAS and CMS credit survives scrutiny of who decided the detector designs. He also raises whether to wait for the redefinition of the second.
responses.response: On founders, I cannot confirm from the files that the founders reading survives scrutiny of who made the decisive design choices, since ATLAS and CMS were built by thousands and several people had real claims to the design. That is exactly why I moved to B031 and why I do not insist on my own opening ballot. On waiting for the redefinition, I would not wait: the redefinition is a decision of the metrology community that depends on the clocks having already been shown to work, which they have. A prize in 2026 recognises what was done; the redefinition would be a consequence. I would, however, accept his request that the citation name the lattice so the prize is not seen as pre-announcing a redefinition.

responses.point: Johansson prefers B031 on discovery-first, instrument-second grounds, notes that the pair leaves out other lattice-clock contributors, and asks whether a precision-measurement instrument counts as a discovery under Nobel's will.
responses.response: I agree with the discovery-first framing and I think the right test is whether the instrument opens new physics, not whether it is an instrument. The lattice clock passes it: millimetre-scale redshift, many-body spin-exchange inside the clock, and limits on varying constants and dark-matter couplings are physics results that were not accessible before. I would be more cautious than he is about calling the clock premature or complete: the strongest applications are still to come. On the contributors outside the pair, I would let the record be checked and not assume it favours two names, but I would not let the check alone break the prize, since every Nobel in a large field leaves out someone defensible.

uncertainties: Whether the committee's experts can confirm from the record that the priority of Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Oates and Hinkley does not alter a Katori and Ye credit; I am relying on memory.
Whether a majority accepts a precision-measurement scheme as a discovery in the sense of Nobel's will, given the 2005 and 2012 prizes in the same area.
Whether the committee prefers to wait for the formal redefinition of the second, which I do not think is necessary.
Whether the unresolved pairing question and the missing first experimental author make B024 premature, or only imperfect, in 2026; I cannot judge this myself and defer to condensed-matter colleagues.
statement.conflict_note: No change to my round-1 disclosure. I have no link to Katori, Ye or the lattice-clock groups. I am in the PAMELA, Fermi-LAT and XL-Calibur collaborations, none of which is on the shortlist, and I trained in particle physics at CERN, which is a general community connection to B005 but not to ATLAS or CMS. I am close to the IceCube field as an astroparticle physicist and would take extra care with B040, which I no longer list as an alternative. As chair I note that Lindroth, Olsson and Kroll have disclosed proximity to the atomic-physics and Tokyo or JILA networks; I do not regard these as conflicts requiring recusal.
